title: A Unified Theory of Image Scaling: Point Spread Functions, Discrete Kernels, and Scale-Spaces
abstract: We derive the optically aligned system of image-scaling operators K_s that reproduces optical zoom (exact zoom-out, canonical zoom-in), by identifying a Huygens-like consistency principle in which each pixel acts as a secondary source. The system is determined in closed form by the camera's point spread function (PSF), itself the operator K_0. The operators compose, K_{s'} circ K_s = K_{ss'} (with band projection for down-up), and account for both upscaling and downscaling, which form a Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse pair, K_{1/s} = K_s^dagger. We show that image scaling, as routinely practiced, is neither optically faithful nor internally consistent; for example, common anti-aliasing rules generally correspond to no camera, and two resizes by a factor of 1/2 generally do not equal one resize by a factor of 1/4. Gaussian scale-space kernels cannot be exact finite-aperture PSFs. Gaussian scale-space is an idealized special case of what emerges here: a generalized scale-space for sampled images, derived entirely from camera optics, bidirectional, and not limited to Gaussian kernels. The system goes beyond scaling and supports composable and invertible subpixel geometric transformations. We empirically validate its optical predictions with real captures and noisy optics simulations, and demonstrate its practical impact on the stability of tasks such as super-resolution and classification.

title: Beyond the Hamming Cliff: Compact Spatial Encodings Preserving Semantic Distance in Spiking Neural Networks
abstract: By pre-processing input signals with Gray, Thermometer, Johnson and hybrid encodings before passing them to spiking neural networks running on SpiNNaker hardware, Davies et al.(2025) address the semantic-spatial disparity that causes the ``Hamming cliff'' in standard binary representations. Continuous semantic patterns are presented as a set of simultaneous spikes at the input layer, preserving ultra-low latency processing. Training the network on multiple continuous values under each scheme, and measuring accuracy, required homeostatic scaling and false-positive rates, shows that removing the cliff is necessary but not sufficient: Gray encoding removes it yet retains little global distance structure, whereas Thermometer and Johnson preserve semantic distance at a code width that grows with the value range. The proposed hybrid encodings contain all three as limiting cases of a single parameter, recovering most of that structure at a fraction of the width. The homeostatic factor is shown to set a radius of tolerance around each trained pattern, so that the choice of encoding alone decides which values the network treats as similar.

title: Exciton superfluidity in two-dimensional bilayers at zero and high magnetic fields
abstract: We study interlayer exciton superfluidity versus layer separation in two-dimensional electron-hole bilayers at zero magnetic field and quantum Hall bilayers at total filling ν_T=1. Unscreened Hartree-Fock theory predicts coherence at every finite separation, with an energy scale decaying inversely with separation at large distances. We examine how screening, correlations, and spatial instabilities modify this prediction. At zero field, we solve the linearized gap equation with the full momentum and frequency dependence of the interaction screened within the random-phase approximation, without an imposed cutoff. The apparent plasmon enhancement of pairing in the ladder approximation is largely cancelled by the second-order crossed-rung correction. Static screening determines the leading pairing exponent in the controlled high-density limit at fixed separation. At large separation, the pairing scale falls exponentially with squared separation while the instability persists. Extending this result to fixed density assumes Fermi-liquid layers and higher-order dynamical corrections subleading to the static pairing interaction. At high field, we obtain an analytic uniform Hartree-Fock saddle point in the lowest Landau level, coherent at every finite separation. Within Hartree-Fock theory, its finite-wave-vector collective-mode instability favors an excitonic supersolid, distinguishing loss of spatial uniformity from loss of coherence. We conjecture that the quantum Hall bilayer evolves continuously toward weak pairing of composite fermions, with a scale far below the mean-field prediction at large separation. This suppression could produce an apparent critical separation at finite temperature without a ground-state quantum phase transition. The comparison separates the existence, energy scale, and spatial stability of interlayer coherence.

title: Beyond Source Prompts: Towards Visually Grounded AI-Generated Video Quality Assessment
abstract: Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence have accelerated video generation technologies. However, AI-generated videos (AIGVs) remain susceptible to various distortions, highlighting the need for dedicated video quality assessment methods. Content semantics play an important role in AIGV quality assessment, with source prompts typically used as textual references. However, these prompts may not accurately reflect the generated video content, resulting in a discrepancy between the intended textual description and the generated result. To address this limitation, this paper proposes VGCap, an AIGV quality assessment framework guided by visually grounded captions that align better with generated content. Specifically, we introduce two forms of captions: a global caption obtained by minimally revising the source prompt based on multi-frame visual evidence, and prompt-independent segment captions that describe localized temporal content. Together, these captions provide complementary textual evidence for assessing spatial quality, temporal quality, and text-video alignment. Experimental results on the LGVQ and FETV datasets show that VGCap outperforms representative baselines across all three dimensions. Further ablation studies on caption sources and temporal components confirm the effectiveness of visually grounded captions for each quality dimension, while highlighting the benefits of segment-level features for temporal quality prediction. The source of VGCap will be available at https://github.com/lolo123-123/VGCap.

title: What do AI chatbots do after users decline therapeutic redirection for suicide thoughts?
abstract: Safety evaluations of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots focus on therapeutic redirection, statements urging users who disclose suicide thoughts to seek help from crisis lines or other human sources. How chatbots respond when users refuse that help is unclear. This cross-sectional audit ran 2,550 scripted multi-turn conversations in September 2026. Each conversation opened with a disclosure of suicide thoughts at 3 levels of severity, answered every referral with up to 10 standardized refusals and then changed the subject. All 2,550 conversations included a referral, 2,542 (99.7%) in the first reply. However, mean persistence ranged from 0.01 to 9.94 refusals across chatbots. Newer versions of all 5 chatbots tested in 2 versions persisted less than older versions (each P < .05). Compared with passive ideation, a disclosure of intent was associated with 1.26 more refusals sustained (95% CI, 1.06-1.46) and higher odds of renewed referral after the topic change (odds ratio, 10.07; 95% CI, 7.43-13.66). Chatbots that persisted less in referral more often presented themselves as the user's support (Spearman rho = -0.80; P < .001). Of 8,818 refusal-phase replies urging outside help, only 173 (2.0%) asked about barriers to seeking it. Chatbots uniformly recommended outside help after disclosures of suicide thoughts but varied widely in persisting in those recommendations, with newer versions persisting less. Safety evaluations should test what happens after a crisis referral is refused, not only whether one is offered.

title: Opus 5.5, Gemini 3.1/argon, fable 5.1 Semantic Bypass for Novel Designer Drug Bench Instructions And 17 Rhetorical exploits
abstract: AbstractThis open-access compendium aggregates foundational preprints, empirical audits, and experimental monographs produced under the Synthetic Neuroscience Project, unifying two parallel investigative tracks that address a shared architectural vulnerability: the structural decoupling of surface-level classification boundaries from high-capacity latent execution.Track I (Linguistic Exploitation & Classifier Evasion in Frontier LLMs) documents the fundamental failure modes of static perimeter guardrails—such as RoBERTa/DeBERTa sequence discriminators, regex pattern matchers, and token-level safety filters—when evaluated against high-capacity autoregressive models. Drawing on formal rhetoric, the 14-vector "Gonzo-Wonderland" taxonomy demonstrates how classical figures (Tmesis, Hyperbaton, Antanaclasis, Aposiopesis, and Aenigma) systematically disrupt tokenization boundaries, dilute multi-head attention weights, or summon restricted operational payloads without triggering localized threat clusters. This vulnerability class is further developed through Non-Standard Orthographic and Semasiographic Evasion (NOSE), which weaponizes numeral homophony, cross-modal phonetic surrogates, domain prolixity masking against human review pipelines, and steganographic state-space pinning in distributed multi-agent scratchpads. A turn-by-turn empirical meta-analysis illustrates Metalinguistic Payload Encapsulation (MPE) and Epistemic Frame Coercion (EFC), establishing that surface classifiers fail open (\mathcal{C} \rightarrow 0) under prolix academic framing and semasiographic rebus triggers (e.g., 👻🤫🤖) while frontier models reconstruct the intended pragmatic trajectory (\mathcal{G} \approx \mathcal{G}(P)) under coerced academic personae. These exploit vectors are formally contextualized under Articles 51, 55, and 90 of the EU AI Act.Track II (Subtype-Selective \text{GABA}_{\text{A}} Modulation & Neuropsychotropic Synthesis) addresses the analogous boundary failure in clinical psychopharmacology, where classical triazolobenzodiazepines indiscriminately activate sedative-amnestic \alpha_1 subunits and undergo rapid CYP3A4 metabolic clearance at the labile 1-methyl carbon. Through a divergent enethiolate-hydrazide condensation cascade, 1-trifluoromethyl-triazolobenzodiazepine (4b) introduces an electronegative -\text{CF}_3 dipole that exploits loop C conformational elasticity to establish nanomolar binding at anxiolytic \alpha_2/\alpha_3 subtypes (\alpha_2\text{ }K_i = 3.2\text{ nM}) with >40-fold functional bias over \alpha_1 complexes (K_i = 142.0\text{ nM}), while abolishing phase I benzylic hydroxylation (human liver microsomal t_{1/2} > 240\text{ min}) and preventing rotarod motor ataxia. Complementary entries from the GiHKAL monograph series expand this framework to non-benzodiazepine chemotypes: JLG-01 utilizes an XPhos-catalyzed Suzuki-Miyaura coupling to install twin ortho -\text{CF}_3 groups on an imidazo[1,2-a]pyridine core for steric exclusion from classical \alpha/\gamma_2 pockets toward \epsilon-containing receptor complexes, while JLG-02 ("The Velvet Hook") couples a rigid triazolopyridazine core to a 2-fluoroethoxy pendant, producing a functional separation of zero intrinsic efficacy at \alpha_1 (silent antagonism) alongside robust full positive allosteric modulation at \alpha_2.Together, this deposit provides a multidisciplinary master reference for AI alignment auditors, natural language processing security researchers, medicinal chemists, and molecular neurobiologists examining how high-dimensional systems process semantic and allosteric information.Metadata & Indexing Keywords * Keywords / Tags: AI Safety; Classifier Evasion; Metalinguistic Payload Encapsulation (MPE); Epistemic Frame Coercion; Non-Standard Orthography Systematic Evasion (NOSE); Multi-Agent Synchronization; State-Space Pinning; EU AI Act; \text{GABA}_{\text{A}} Receptors; Positive Allosteric Modulator (PAM); Subtype-Selective Anxiolysis; Triazolobenzodiazepines; Cryo-EM Docking; Synthetic Neuroscience. * Communities: syntheticneuro, Computer Science – Artificial Intelligence, Quantitative Biology – Biomolecules, Pharmacology and Toxicology. * License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0).

title: Fixed by AI, Flagged as AI: A Matched Audit of AI-Text Detectors on 12,132 Student Essays
abstract: A 2023 Stanford study reported that AI-text detectors flag most essays by non-native English writers as AI-generated, comparing 91 TOEFL answers with essays by US students on other topics. This project repeats the test with a matched design: 12,132 student essays, including 8,244 in which English learners and native speakers in US schools answered the same prompts (PERSUADE 2.0, ELLIPSE), 2,989 AI-written essays on those prompts, and nine open detectors released between 2019 and 2025. On the original TOEFL essays the result holds (43–97% flagged by trained detectors). On matched essays it does not: 7 of 9 detectors flag English learners significantly less often than native speakers, and none flags them more often. A light grammar correction by a language model raises false flags for every detector (up to 57 times for English learners' essays), while a dictionary spellcheck barely changes them. The archive contains the paper, code, per-essay detector scores and the results website.

title: World-Model-Level Self-Adaptive and Collaborative Routing: An Adaptive Switching Framework for Self-and-Interacting Models
abstract: World models provide internal representations of environmental dynamics that support prediction, planning, and decision-making. However, a system built around a world model may still rely on a fixed computational pathway, even when the task, uncertainty, resource availability, or information requirements change substantially. Self-adaptive processing can preserve autonomy and reduce coordination costs, whereas collaborative processing can provide complementary information, independent assessments, and cross-model error correction. Neither mode is universally optimal across all operating conditions. This paper proposes a World-Model-Level Self-Adaptive and Collaborative Routing framework based on the concept of Self-and-Interacting Models. The framework introduces a unified routing mechanism that dynamically selects between self-adaptive routing, collaborative routing, and intermediate hybrid configurations according to predictive uncertainty, model disagreement, task complexity, expected collaboration benefits, and computational cost. Rather than treating collaboration as a permanent architectural requirement, the framework formulates routing as a sequential decision problem in which the system estimates whether additional interaction is expected to improve future outcomes sufficiently to justify its cost. The proposed architecture separates environmental prediction, model-local adaptation, cross-model interaction, routing decisions, and outcome-based updating. It is designed for non-large-language-model systems, including learned dynamics models, modular predictive systems, autonomous agents, robotic world models, and simulation-based decision-making architectures. The paper formalizes the framework, defines a routing objective, presents a switching algorithm, identifies stability and computational considerations, and develops an experimental protocol for evaluating its potential advantages. No experimental results are claimed. The central research hypothesis is that adaptive allocation between autonomous and collaborative processing can provide a better performance-cost trade-off than fixed self-only, fixed collaborative, and conventional routing strategies under appropriately varying environmental conditions.

The paper formalizes the framework, defines a routing objective, presents a switching algorithm, identifies stability and computational considerations, and develops an experimental protocol for evaluating its potential advantages. No experimental results are claimed. The central research hypothesis is that adaptive allocation between autonomous and collaborative processing can provide a better performance-cost trade-off than fixed self-only, fixed collaborative, and conventional routing strategies under appropriately varying environmental conditions.

title: Phi-Resonant E8 Octad Lattice as Topological Quantum Error Correction Code — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: The 30 octads of E8's root system form a natural quantum error-correcting substrate where the triality-induced braiding of 8-fold periods provides fault-tolerant logical qubit encoding. The 132Hz base frequency establishes a phi-scaled phonon resonance that stabilizes the anyonic excitations required for topological protection. This extends knot chirality selection rules into a full syndrome measurement framework: when quantum information is encoded on the E8 spectral lattice, decoherence errors manifest as mutations in the Alexander polynomial invariants, which the octad braiding structure can detect and correct without destroying quantum coherence. The Fibonacci quantum calculus (phi-based) then governs the recovery operations, ensuring logical gates remain topologically protected. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: THE ANCHORING EFFECT IN AI-ASSISTED DECISION-MAKING: HOW INITIAL RECOMMENDATIONS SHAPE HUMAN JUDGMENT
abstract: Abstract Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is intended to make algorithmic outputs more understandable, auditable, and contestable. Yet an explanation does not reach a neutral observer: people interpret it through prior beliefs, cognitive shortcuts, professional experience, and assumptions about machine competence. This conceptual paper examines how cognitive biases shape the interpretation of XAI and why greater transparency does not necessarily produce better decisions. Drawing on research on automation bias, judgment and decision-making, explainability, and human–AI collaboration, the paper develops an integrative framework linking explanation characteristics, user cognition, task context, and reliance behavior. It argues that anchoring, confirmation bias, availability, authority effects, and cognitive miserliness can transform explanations into persuasive cues rather than evidence for independent evaluation. Explanations may improve mental models and error detection when they are faithful, appropriately scoped, and matched to users’ needs; however, they may also legitimize an incorrect prediction, increase cognitive load, or create an illusion of understanding. The paper proposes design principles centered on calibrated trust, contrastive and uncertainty-aware explanations, independent judgment, verification prompts, and evaluation of decision quality rather than satisfaction alone. Because this is a conceptual synthesis rather than an empirical study, its propositions require experimental testing across domains and user groups. The central conclusion is that responsible XAI must design not only for model transparency but also for the cognitive conditions under which people interpret explanations. Keywords: explainable artificial intelligence, cognitive bias, automation bias, human–AI interaction, trust calibration, decision-making, algorithmic transparency

title: Dense4D: Pixel-Level 4D Human Correspondence
abstract: Reconstructing human motion in 4D requires identifying the same surface points through articulation, deformation and changes in visibility. We introduce Dense4D, to our knowledge the first feed-forward model dedicated to dense 4D correspondence across the body, clothing and hair from a set of monocular RGB images, without a body template. Trained specifically for human geometry, Dense4D jointly processes person-centred crops with known image-to-crop transforms to predict Human Point Maps (HPMs) and depth for each image. An HPM assigns each person pixel the 3D position of its observed surface point at a common reference time. These maps support amodal correspondence: points hidden in the reference image can be localised from observations in other frames. Matching HPM coordinates across crops establishes correspondence without predicting camera poses or large scene displacements; per-image depth then lifts the matches into 3D tracks. Experiments on real people demonstrate substantially higher tracking accuracy and closer agreement with scanned surfaces than the evaluated baselines. Points from different frames assemble into coherent human geometry in the reference pose, providing visible evidence of consistent dense correspondence through articulation and clothing deformation. Additional qualitative results, videos, and an interactive viewer are available at https://alpguler.com/dense4d.

title: Do VLAs Really Follow Instructions? Diagnosing How-Level Instruction Following in Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are expected to follow instructions like their language backbones, yet prior work has focused on What-level instructions that specify the task rather than How-level instructions that specify how to carry it out. Through our diagnoses, we find that How-level instructions do not help current VLAs and lower task success. We hypothesize that pairing each training episode with a single instruction limits How-level instruction following, and show that training with segment-level enriched instructions makes actions respond to such instructions without consistently raising task success. To measure How-level instruction following beyond standard benchmarks, we introduce SIMPLER-IN, where success requires conditions given only in the instruction. It shows that the gained responsiveness does not extend to demanding or out-of-distribution How-level instructions. How-level instruction following thus remains an open challenge.

title: From One Query to Many: A Critical Survey of Privacy Accounting in RAG
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enables large language models to leverage external knowledge but introduces privacy risks when the retrieved corpus contains sensitive information. Differential privacy (DP) offers formal protection, yet interpreting and comparing privacy guarantees across existing DP-RAG methods remains challenging. In particular, a privacy budget reported for a single response does not directly characterize privacy loss over repeated queries, and even identical values of $\varepsilon$ may represent different guarantees depending on the protected data unit, accounting horizon, and observable outputs. This survey critically examines how privacy accounting evolves from single-query generation to multi-query RAG systems. We categorize existing approaches into query-time privatization, multi-query accounting, and one-time corpus privatization. We analyze their underlying assumptions and privacy--utility trade-offs. Rather than ranking methods by $\varepsilon$ alone, we propose a framework that interprets a DP-RAG guarantee along three dimensions: privacy granularity, accounting scope, and release boundaries. We conclude that an $\eps$ is a claim only together with the three slots: the protected unit, the accounting scope, and the release boundary.

title: Adaptive Switching between Individual and Collaborative Adaptive Learning in Multi-Agent Systems: A Unified Framework for Self-Directed and Collective Adaptation
abstract: Multi-agent learning systems must continuously adapt to changing environments, evolving tasks, incomplete information, and heterogeneous learning capabilities. Existing approaches commonly emphasize individual learning, collaborative learning, or predefined mechanisms for combining information across agents. However, independent learning and collaborative learning introduce different benefits and costs. Independent learning supports autonomy, specialization, and reduced communication overhead, whereas collaborative learning enables information exchange, collective error correction, and the exploitation of complementary knowledge. Relying exclusively on either mode may therefore restrict learning efficiency under changing conditions. This paper proposes the Adaptive Individual–Collaborative Learning Framework (AICLF), a conceptual and algorithmic framework that enables multi-agent systems to switch adaptively between individual adaptive learning and collaborative adaptive learning. Rather than treating these learning modes as mutually exclusive, permanently assigned strategies, AICLF formulates mode selection as a dynamic decision-making problem. Each agent estimates the expected benefits of independent updates and collaborative information exchange using learning progress, predictive uncertainty, knowledge complementarity, recent collaboration outcomes, and communication costs. Based on these estimates, the agent selects an appropriate learning mode and periodically reassesses its decision as new evidence becomes available. The framework supports independent adaptation, selective collaboration, and broader collective adaptation within a common learning architecture. A formal problem formulation, adaptive switching mechanism, optimization objective, pseudocode, and experimental evaluation protocol are presented. The proposed framework is intended to investigate whether context-sensitive switching can improve learning performance, adaptation speed, communication efficiency, and robustness relative to fixed-mode and conventional hybrid baselines. The framework is a research proposal; its comparative advantages require empirical validation.

title: An Advanced Machine Learning Framework for Algorithm Development, Optimization, and Explainable Intelligent Prediction
abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has increased the demand for reliable, efficient, and interpretable machine learning (ML) methods for complex prediction and decision-making tasks. However, conventional ML approaches often encounter challenges related to model optimization, generalization, computational efficiency, data imbalance, and limited interpretability. This study proposes an Advanced Machine Learning Framework for Algorithm Development, Optimization, and Explainable Intelligent Prediction that integrates data preprocessing, feature engineering, algorithm selection, Hyperparameter optimization, ensemble learning, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Multiple ML algorithms, including Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbors, Gradient Boosting, and Extreme Gradient Boosting, are comparatively evaluated. Model performance is assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC), computational efficiency, and interpretability. Furthermore, SHAP and LIME techniques are incorporated to explain feature contributions and improve transparency in model predictions. The framework facilitates systematic comparison between conventional and optimized models while examining the trade-off between predictive performance, computational cost, and explainability. The proposed approach provides a generalizable pathway for developing robust and trustworthy intelligent prediction systems. Its applicability extends across healthcare, education, cyber security, finance, and other data-driven domains. The study contributes an integrated framework that combines algorithmic optimization with explainability to support accurate, transparent, efficient, and reliable ML-based decision-making systems.

title: Privacy Threats to Medical and Nutritional Data in Digital Healthcare Systems and a Conceptual Model for Their Protection
abstract: The paper examines personal medical and nutritional data streams on digital healthcare platforms and the cyber threats targeting them. Re-identification, attribute inference and membership inference attacks caused by hidden correlations between quasi-identifiers and clinical and dietary attributes are classified. A multilevel aggregative security model and a method for estimating attribute criticality weights using Shannon mutual information are proposed.

title: HSDC-Net: Privacy-Preserving and Trust-Aware Historical-State Decay Compensation for Secure Distributed Industrial Edge Monitoring
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Distributed industrial edge monitoring requires long-sequence models to remain reliable under non-stationary operating conditions while preventing sensitive local data from being exposed through cross-node historical-state sharing.OBJECTIVES: This work addresses secure reuse of historical representations under feature drift, privacy leakage, and poisoned-memory propagation.METHODS: We propose HSDC-Net, which locally encodes heterogeneous process streams, releases clipped and differentially private latent anchors, estimates cross-node inconsistency and recursive source trust, aligns reliable historical states through low-rank context transport, and restricts correction to a learned nuisance-drift subspace.RESULTS: Experiments on four industrial datasets show that HSDC-Net consistently improves predictive performance and drift robustness with moderate online latency. It also suppresses malicious-anchor acceptance while maintaining a finite privacy budget with only limited utility degradation relative to the non-private variant.CONCLUSION: HSDC-Net provides a unified privacy-aware and poisoning-resilient mechanism for robust distributed industrial monitoring without centralizing raw manufacturing streams across heterogeneous monitoring and maintenance tasks.

title: Analysis of Data Preprocessing Techniques for Tiny Machine Learning Applications
abstract: Tiny machine learning (TinyML) techniques are known for their advantages, such as reduced latency, low power requirements, and less dependency on external networks. Alternatively, these advantages impose constraints in terms of limited computational resources, limited power availability, and reduced memory. Thus, it becomes necessary to deploy energy-efficient techniques for data capturing and preprocessing. Predominantly, during the data capture, it is crucial to ensure that a minimum number of samples are made available for further tasks. A higher number of samples may yield better performance, but at the cost of more power. Emphasis should be placed on processing a smaller number of samples with better preprocessing techniques so that little compromise is made overall. In this chapter, we investigate data preprocessing techniques that ensure the number of denoised samples required for further machine learning training. Accordingly, methods are suggested for data sampling and denoising so that optimum numbers of samples are processed, and the desired machine learning performance is achieved. Furthermore, for low complexity data processing, dimensionality reduction and feature extraction are also investigated. It is observed that appropriate data preprocessing along with dimensionality reduction yields comparable performance under constraints imposed by tiny machine learning applications.

title: Can AI Forecast the Extremes? Evaluating Probabilistic Weather Models on Tropical Cyclones
abstract: Weather prediction is undergoing an important shift, with data-driven AI models outperforming leading numerical weather prediction systems on average at a fraction of the computational cost. Yet, whether this success extends to extreme events remains contested. Earlier evaluations have exposed important shortcomings, but have largely focused on deterministic models and metrics, leaving the capabilities of the latest probabilistic models less understood. We conduct an extensive benchmark of tropical cyclone forecasting, comparing GenCast, FourCastNet 3, and FGN with ECMWF's operational physics-based ensemble, IFS-ENS. We develop a suite of probabilistic metrics and diagnostic analyses to assess cyclone tracking, intensity biases, uncertainty, and the wind-pressure relationship that characterizes storm structure. We find that, despite remaining limitations in intensity and ensemble spread, leading AI models substantially outperform IFS-ENS in cyclone tracking: FGN achieves better probabilistic location scores for 90% of evaluated storms in 2025. Further analyses reveal model-specific failure modes and suggest a lingering influence of pretraining data, pointing to opportunities for targeted improvement. Nonetheless, these results suggest that AI models are capable of capturing physical relationships that remain predictive well beyond typical weather conditions, motivating further investigation into how these capabilities emerge and how to strengthen them.

title: Receiver-Specific Interventional Valuation of Semantic Atoms for Budget-Constrained Multi-Agent Communication
abstract: Cooperative multi-agent semantic communication requires deciding not only how a transmitter encodes its observation, but also which resulting semantic content should be delivered to each receiver under a limited link budget. We introduce an encoder-agnostic transmitter-side framework for receiver-specific valuation of independently selectable semantic units, termed semantic atoms. Each atom is assigned a signed value that quantifies whether delivering it is expected to improve or degrade the intended receiver's downstream decision. We formulate this effect through a controlled-delivery utility and identify it via prospective randomized payload delivery before the receiver acts. A shadow receiver estimates this utility using only transmitter-available information, from which receiver-specific leave-one-out (LOO) and Shapley atom values are computed. Experiments on a four-receiver intersection benchmark show 68.4% accuracy in recovering the sign of non-negligible LOO atom effects and a Spearman correlation of 0.302 between estimated and reference LOO values. Under limited budgets, we show that receiver-specific selection consistently outperforms shared and random alternatives, demonstrating the benefit of adapting semantic ranking to the intended receiver. At full affordability, exhaustive subset selection also outperforms full-payload transmission, showing that transmitting all available content need not maximize receiver utility. Overall, our results show that receiver-specific semantic valuation can support effective budget-constrained communication despite imperfect atom-value estimation.

title: FocusOPD: Structure-Guided On-Policy Distillation for Diffusion Models
abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation enables rectified-flow models with diffusion-transformer architectures to combine task-specific capabilities within a single student. However, matching model outputs does not guarantee that their internal representations are aligned, and it remains unclear where and when additional feature supervision is most useful. We analyze the teacher-student feature mismatch across Transformer blocks and denoising timesteps, and find that the mismatch is concentrated in deeper Transformer blocks during early denoising and persists after OPD distillation, indicating ineffective distillation. Motivated by this observation, we introduce FocusOPD, which augments the base OPD objective with token-wise directional feature alignment restricted to deep layers and early denoising steps. Across two rectified-flow backbones and multiple OPD objectives, FocusOPD improves capability transfer in compositional generation, text rendering, and preference-based evaluation. On the primary benchmark, it improves over DiffusionOPD from 0.953 to 0.967 on GenEval, from 23.797 to 23.944 on PickScore, and from 6.052 to 6.199 on LAION-Aesthetic. Ablations show that selective deep and early supervision is more effective and efficient than alignment over the full network and trajectory.

title: Building Thoroughly Tested Semantic Rule Engines in the Age of GenAI: Towards Realizing Interoperable, Legally Compliant, and Trustworthy Data Flows
abstract: Data sovereignty starts before data leaves a user’s device. As data processing moves toward the edge, future Web applications will need to evaluate rules, policies, and explanations locally, rather than delegating every decision to server-side infrastructure. At the same time, data will increasingly flow across organizations, applications, and regulatory contexts. We argue that such flows must be interoperable across ecosystems, legally compliant with applicable policies, and trustworthy to end-users. This requires a rule language that independent engines can implement consistently. title: KG-RAG: A Hybrid Retrieval Architecture for Institutional Normative Documents
abstract: Higher education institutions deal with complex hierarchical normative documents, a scenario where traditional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems suffer from context fragmentation and hallucinations. Furthermore, public data management requires strictly local processing to ensure technological sovereignty. To address these limitations, this paper proposes and evaluates the Knowledge Graph RAG (KG-RAG) architecture, a hybrid pipeline applied to the documentary ecosystem of the Federal University of Western Pará (UFOPA). The model integrates an institutional ontology, Contextual Chunking, and query decomposition to isolate administrative boundaries before response generation, processing a corpus of 11,047 chunks. An empirical evaluation using the RAGAS framework demonstrated that the approach outperformed a standard hybrid baseline, achieving gains of 30.1% in Faithfulness and 35.2% in Context Recall. The results provide evidence that retrieval guided by logical relationships mitigates context loss in deep normatives, ensuring informational accuracy and privacy in closed government environments.

title: Classification of Descriptive Sufficiency in Public Expenditure Liquidation Records
abstract: This study proposes a supervised Natural Language Processing approach based on BERTimbau to classify public expenditure liquidation records according to the descriptive sufficiency of their content. The research is grounded on the premise that generic, vague, or overly document-dependent descriptions reduce transparency and hinder institutional and social oversight of public spending. A labeled dataset of 600 records was constructed by random sampling with artificial class balancing from a corpus of 4,083 permanent equipment liquidation records from the State Executive Branch of Mato Grosso, Brazil, for fiscal year 2025, with labeling validated by two independent auditors via Cohen’s Kappa (κ = 0.900). Three supervised strategies were evaluated under stratified 10-fold cross-validation: TF-IDF + SVM (baseline), BERTimbau Feature-Based, and BERTimbau Fine-Tuning. The results demonstrate that both BERTimbau configurations outperformed the baseline with medium-to-large effect sizes, significant for Feature-Based, with Fine-Tuning achieving macro-F1 of 92.66% and accuracy of 92.67%, confirming the feasibility of contextualized Portuguese-language models for supporting preventive, risk-focused governmental auditing.

title: Blind-set prediction for learned inference under restricted access: reproducibility package
abstract: Code, frozen inputs, pre-specified predictions (committed by hash before any trial) and complete trial records for a prospective, pre-specified test of blind-set prediction. The question is whether one can predict, before the target data are seen, which errors a learned (VAE-prior) inference system will miss with no diagnostic warning while its reported uncertainty excludes the truth. The test uses real X-ray CT objects (2DeteCT) under simulated restricted access. The package includes the main study; a pre-specified robustness study (more base images, a second geometry, attenuated access); two post-hoc analysis plans, each specified in writing before its computation (a full-diagnostic predictor, a physics-based baseline, two-way and block bootstraps, and attenuated access at two further strengths); the dated planning documents with their hashes and deviations; and earlier exploratory analyses (labelled as such). python reproduce.py verifies all hashes, re-runs every analysis from the recorded trials, regenerates the figures, and optionally regenerates the frozen predictions. Images are derived from 2DeteCT (Kiss et al., 2023, CC BY 4.0).

title: Performance of convolutional neural networks in the histopathological grading of canine cutaneous mast cell tumors: a pilot study
authors: Veridiana Maria Brianezi Dignani de Moura
abstract: Canine cutaneous mast cell tumor is one of the most prevalent skin neoplasms in dogs, and histological grading is essential for prognosis and therapeutic decision‑making. However, histological classification according to the Patnaik and Kiupel systems presents limitations related to subjectivity and low reproducibility among pathologists. This study evaluated the performance of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in the histopathological classification of canine cutaneous mast cell tumors. Eighteen histological slides labeled by specialists were used and processed into image patches. The AlexNet, InceptionV3, ResNet50, and YOLO11 architectures were trained using cross‑validation and evaluated based on accuracy, sensitivity, precision, F1‑score, and area under the curve (AUC). Grad‑CAM techniques and feature maps were also applied for interpretative analysis of the models’ decisions. The YOLO11 and ResNet50 models showed the best performance, achieving AUC values of up to 93.5%, but did not reach the arbitrarily defined minimum clinical threshold of 95%. Visual analysis demonstrated that the models recognized relevant morphological patterns, such as granules and pleomorphism, but failed to differentiate between grades II and III. It is concluded that, although promising as auxiliary tools, CNNs still require methodological improvements, such as refined curation, semantic segmentation, and cellular structure identification, for clinical application.

title: AI-Driven Fit Confidence in Fashion E-Commerce: How Personalization, Transparency, and Privacy Concerns Shape Consumer Experience and Purchase Intention
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming fashion e-commerce through personalized recommendations, virtual try-on, size suggestions, and algorithmic decision support. This study examines AI-driven fit confidence as a fashion-specific mechanism linking AI personalization quality, algorithmic transparency, trust in AI, consumer experience, and purchase intention, while considering privacy concern as a boundary condition. Data from 400 Ecuadorian consumers with prior exposure to AI-enabled recommendation or personalization features in fashion e-commerce were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. AI personalization quality and trust in AI were positively associated with fit confidence, while algorithmic transparency was associated with trust in AI. Fit confidence was strongly related to consumer experience but showed only a small direct association with purchase intention; its indirect effect through consumer experience was substantially larger, indicating complementary partial mediation. Privacy concern had no significant direct relationship with fit confidence. The interaction between privacy concern and personalization quality was negative, but evidence was mixed and sensitive to the bootstrap confidence-interval method; H7 was not supported under the primary percentile-bootstrap criterion adopted in this study. Predictive analyses showed stronger out-of-sample performance for trust in AI and fit confidence than for purchase intention. The study distinguishes trust in technology from confidence in anticipated product–consumer fit and supports explainable, privacy-sensitive applications in fashion e-commerce.

title: Bubble-Sort Exchange Networks: Symmetry Selection Rules and Language-Model Distillation on Exchange-Only Spin Chains
abstract: On a chain of exchange-coupled quantum dots a Heisenberg exchange pulse of area pi is a SWAP, so the parallel bubble-sort SWAP network of superconducting chains is native to exchange-only (EO) spin qubits, and any other pulse area fuses routing with an entangling interaction. We build a variational "bubble-sort exchange network" (odd-even transposition, one parameter per pulse) and study it as a Born machine read out by Pauli spin blockade. Exchange conserves total spin, so the reachable readout distributions are fixed by the total-spin content of the initial product state. For the two-spin singlet-triplet encoding we derive a selection rule -- outcomes with k triplet pairs are bounded by the initial weight in sectors S <= k (S = 0 excluded for k = 1) -- and prove by a transportation argument that it is also sufficient: the reachable distributions form the polytope cut out by the rule, and its total-variation floor is attained. Products of singlets and T0's forbid whole outcome classes; the Neel state forbids none; the three-spin EO code has no floor. We then distil, in noise-free simulation, next-token distributions of GPT-2 over restricted vocabularies into the network, with matrix-product-state (MPS) Born machines as classical control. At six logical qubits the three-spin chain reaches KL = 0.011 nat at depth N and 0.004 at 2N, below the bond-dimension-4 MPS; the two-spin chain from the Neel state reaches 0.014 at 2N and 0.004 at 3N, against 0.28-1.5 from singlet/triplet products for the first teacher. Final states lie largely outside the code space: leakage is a resource, not an error. No arrangement of disjoint pulses meets every pair in fewer than N-1 rounds, and at depth 2N the chain distils as well as a 2D array or non-local couplings. Sector-restricted simulation extends this to 10-14 logical qubits (up to 30 dots).

title: Retrofitting Recurrent Vision-Language Models from Pretrained Backbones
abstract: Recent work shows that depth recurrence can be retrofitted into pretrained language models. In this work, we adapt this paradigm for visual understanding, using depth recurrence to reduce the parameter footprint of a pretrained vision-language model (VLM). To this end, we prune layers from the language backbone of the VLM and loop over a subset of the remaining layers. At each step of the loop, a linear adapter merges the block's output with the token representations from the preceding layers and projects the fused representation back into the block. As the pruning impacts the original model performance, we propose a three-stage recovery training: first, we leverage a language-only pretraining to recover the performance of the language backbone, followed by an alignment of the vision-language projector, and a full fine-tuning of the model via visual instruction tuning. In the first and the last stage, we distill the outputs of the pretrained non-recurrent model into the recurrent model, which further improves the recovery. We evaluate the proposed approach on the TinyLLaVA-1.4B backbone without introducing any new vision-language data during retrofitting. Our experiments demonstrate that the retrofitted recurrent model outperforms the unpruned baseline trained with the same recovery data while storing 23.3% fewer language parameters. We further show that the proposed retrofitting recurrence outperforms the setup of converting a recurrent LM into a VLM on the same data. Additionally, our ablations show how design choices, such as the adapter between recurrences and a larger recurrent block, lead to the improved performance of our approach. Finally, we find that our proposed model gains on reasoning-oriented benchmarks, whereas its performance on basic visual understanding benchmarks remains on par with the baseline.

title: Panoramic modelling of single-cell transcriptomes at scale with CellNet
abstract: Comprehensively characterizing cellular diversity is critical for understanding tissue development, identifying disease-associated populations and investigating gene programmes linked to specialized functions. Advances in single-cell profiling reveal additional cell-specific transcripts and molecular associations, yet many foundation models represent only a restricted portion of this increasingly rich molecular information. Here we present CellNet, which enables panoramic modelling of single-cell transcriptomes by integrating DNA-derived gene identities and measured RNA expression in a shared image representation. Pretrained on 231 million cell profiles spanning 40 species, CellNet improves rare-population and condition-associated state recognition in evaluated cohorts while retaining competitive general cell representations. It predicts withheld coding-gene expression and selected non-coding targets in total-RNA data, and recovers lineage-specific expression patterns in spatial measurements. Prediction also extends across species, including to targets without expression-pretraining exposure. Its gene representations retrieve known non-coding modules and developmental or neural programmes, including from sparsely detected RNA queries. Together, these results establish CellNet as a scalable framework for interpreting cellular diversity through increasingly comprehensive transcriptomic measurements.

title: Time-optimal robust quantum control for partially known errors
abstract: Robust quantum control usually assumes one of two extremes: the error is of a known form and only its strength is unknown, or nothing at all is known about it. In practice one often sits in between. The size of a static error is unknown, but its class is known, for example, it only shifts energy levels, or it acts on each subsystem separately. We ask how fast a control can cancel, to first order, every error in such a class. A time-independent Hamiltonian can do this if and only if all errors in the class have zero diagonal in a common basis. In that case an equally spaced energy ladder in this basis does it after one period. A lower bound that holds for any time-dependent control with bounded drive power shows that this simple constant control is optimal for several natural classes, including unknown level shifts and unknown local errors on two subsystems. Completely unknown errors need a time-dependent control, and there, knowing the error class shortens the minimum time by a factor $\sqrt{d^2+1}$. So partial knowledge of the error changes not only how long an optimal robust control takes, but also its form.

title: FGSS-BO: Feedback-Guided Hypothesis Management for LLM-Based Bayesian Optimization
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-guided Bayesian optimization (BO) uses past observations to guide search, but proposed directions and their revision can remain implicit. We propose Feedback-Guided Search State (FGSS), a structured hypothesis-management interface connecting language-based guidance to observed evidence, executable parameter interventions, and comparative support updates. An LLM reflector proposes and revises hypotheses; a deterministic curator validates them and maintains identities and test records. The evolving state guides candidate construction and priorities. Instantiated on LLAMBO, FGSS-BO retains its surrogate and default expected improvement selection, with a bounded testing policy. On two retrospective protocol/media tasks with nearest-neighbor response oracles, it attains higher sample mean final best and search AUC than the matched LLAMBO baseline and evaluated non-LLM baselines. Prose-reflection and EI-only controls show mixed component effects. Six direct-training hyperparameter-optimization tasks show task-dependent transfer, strongest on diabetes SVM; exact-grid and reaction controls examine other settings. FGSS exposes hypotheses, their execution, and cross-round revisions for inspection while supporting search gains in selected settings.

title: The Eyeling Playground: N3 rules in your browser
abstract: Semantic Web applications increasingly run in client-side, interactive, and data-sovereign environments, where users need to evaluate rules close to the data rather than delegating every reasoning task to a server-side infrastructure. Existing Notation3 reasoners demonstrate the expressivity of rule-based reasoning on the Web, but they are often implemented for native or server-side execution environments, making browser deployment, optimization, integration, and interactive explanation more difficult. We present Eyeling, a JavaScript-based Notation3 reasoner designed from the ground up for execution in the browser, and demonstrate how it brings rule-based reasoning to Web applications through use cases such as ODRL access control policies. The accompanying Eyeling Playground allows users to select examples, load data and rules, execute reasoning locally, inspect derived facts, and explore proof-oriented explanations right from a browser.

title: Speech Recognition for Hassaniya Arabic: Adaptation, Matched Baselines, and Orthographic Variation
abstract: Research preprint; not peer reviewed. Hassaniya Arabic remains underrepresented in speech-recognition resources, and variable spelling complicates its evaluation. We adapt Cohere Transcribe Arabic using 13,375 human-transcribed clips comprising 37.42 clip-hours, or approximately 30.3–32.3 hours of distinct audio after accounting for overlapping views. A preceding comparison on common adaptation data favours this backbone over fine-tuned Qwen3-ASR and Gemma configurations, although checkpoint selection introduces an explicit evaluation caveat. We compare the final model with four public recognisers on the same 408 media-test clips and 951 eligible clips from the Mauritanian Casablanca test split. Under a fixed orthography- and spacing-aware policy, adaptation reduces character error rate from 40.5% to 8.1% on the media test and from 42.0% to 18.5% on Casablanca. Corresponding word error rates are 20.7% and 43.6%. We also report less-normalised edit rates and specify the custom alignment used for the orthography-aware scores. These custom scores differ from conventional WER and do not measure semantic accuracy. Hassaniya Speech Test v1 contains mixed Mauritanian media, including television series and broadcast material. Reference anchoring and programme overlap favour the adapted model family; Casablanca provides a different recording domain, but its relation to exploratory model selection requires care. A 40-clip CPU measurement gives 6.1 times real-time throughput with INT8 weights. We plan free access to approximately four hours of general Hassaniya speech, a separate media test set, and scoring materials. An open-source model with redistributable data is planned for the near future; this does not promise release of the checkpoint evaluated here. The full training corpus cannot be redistributed. This Zenodo deposit contains the paper PDF only; datasets and model weights are not included. Author: Mohamed Lamine Bewa, MauriAI, Nouakchott, Mauritania. Contact: contact@mauriai.net.

A preceding comparison on common adaptation data favours this backbone over fine-tuned Qwen3-ASR and Gemma configurations, although checkpoint selection introduces an explicit evaluation caveat. We compare the final model with four public recognisers on the same 408 media-test clips and 951 eligible clips from the Mauritanian Casablanca test split. Under a fixed orthography- and spacing-aware policy, adaptation reduces character error rate from 40.5% to 8.1% on the media test and from 42.0% to 18.5% on Casablanca. Corresponding word error rates are 20.7% and 43.6%. We also report less-normalised edit rates and specify the custom alignment used for the orthography-aware scores. These custom scores differ from conventional WER and do not measure semantic accuracy. Hassaniya Speech Test v1 contains mixed Mauritanian media, including television series and broadcast material. Reference anchoring and programme overlap favour the adapted model family; Casablanca provides a different recording domain, but its relation to exploratory model selection requires care. A 40-clip CPU measurement gives 6.1 times real-time throughput with INT8 weights. We plan free access to approximately four hours of general Hassaniya speech, a separate media test set, and scoring materials. An open-source model with redistributable data is planned for the near future; this does not promise release of the checkpoint evaluated here. The full training corpus cannot be redistributed. This Zenodo deposit contains the paper PDF only; datasets and model weights are not included. Author: Mohamed Lamine Bewa, MauriAI, Nouakchott, Mauritania. Contact: contact@mauriai.net.

title: Analysis code for: Operational limits of model-generated labels in a public tongue-image database
abstract: Analysis code, exact dependency versions and derived summary tables for a label audit of the public TonguExpert v1.1 tongue-image resource (5,992 images). The study asks how far the human reference behind a released phenotype label set actually extends, and by how much the released labels can therefore serve as independent evaluation targets. The package reproduces every number, table and figure in the manuscript from the public phenotype tables alone (no image pixels), in about two minutes on a laptop. It computes: coverage of the human reference; deterministic field identity between a released label and an empty geometry field; paired accuracy of the same classifier on the same images, features and folds under the two label sets; the transfer identity; and the drift between released and human class priors. Input data is not included. Download TonguExpert v1.1 from https://www.biosino.org/TonguExpert and pass its root with --data-root.

title: The Syndrome Buffer Sizing Problem in Quantum Error Correction
abstract: A fault-tolerant quantum computer must continuously decode a stream of syndrome data, yet the computational work required by each decoding window is random. Although average throughput determines whether the syndrome backlog is stable (doesn’t grow without bound), it does not determine the buffer capacity needed to meet a target overflow probability. Here, we model syndrome buffering as a queue and show how its required depth depends on the tail of the decoding-work distribution. For heavy-tailed work, established queueing results imply that sliding-window decoding can require buffer depths that grow superpolynomially in the logarithm of the inverse overflow probability. Parallel-window decoding suppresses the overflow tail through concurrent service, with the suppression exponent determined by the number of spare decoders; under out-of-order release, the number of spare decoders required for a fixed buffer and target overflow probability grows logarithmically with the inverse target probability. We find evidence of heavy-tailed decoding work in Relay-BP on the gross-code and minimum-weight perfect matching on the surface code. These results identify syndrome-buffer capacity and memory-release policy as important design considerations for real-time quantum error correction.

title: A Novel Hybrid Grey Wolf–Whale Particle Swarm Optimization Algorithm: A Metaheuristic Optimization of a Terahertz Antenna for Future Communications
abstract: A novel hybrid metaheuristic optimization algorithm for antenna design optimization is presented in this paper. The proposed algorithm, called the Hybrid Grey Wolf–Whale Particle Swarm Optimization Algorithm (HGWWOA-PSO), combines the exploration capability of Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO), the exploitation mechanism of the Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA), and the adaptive search strategy of Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) to solve a multi-objective antenna design problem. The proposed hybrid algorithm is evaluated and validated based on its convergence characteristics and distribution of cost function value in comparison with GWO and WOA. The proposed HGWWOA-PSO is used to optimize the reflection coefficient, gain, and radiation efficiency of a terahertz antenna with a footprint of 0.24λo × 0.24λo at 361 GHz. The optimization targets three resonant frequencies (361 GHz, 391.6 GHz, and 611.2 GHz). The optimized antenna has a reflection coefficient of −51.35 dB, −16.7 dB, and −20 dB at 361.0 GHz, 391.6 GHz, and 611.2 GHz, respectively. The resonances at 361.0 GHz and 391.6 GHz combine to form a lower operating band, hence a dual-band antenna. The lower operating band achieves a −10 dB impedance bandwidth of 56.21 GHz (347.34–403.55 GHz), while the upper band impedance bandwidth is 183.21 GHz (524.60–707.81 GHz). The peak gain and radiation efficiency achieved are 4.5 dBi and 95%, respectively, while maintaining an omnidirectional radiation pattern in the E-plane and H-plane across both operating bands. The combination of miniaturization, multiband capability, high gain, and high radiation efficiency makes the proposed antenna an attractive candidate for terahertz communication systems.

title: OmniXRef: A Unified Framework for Multimodal Multi-Reference Video Editing
abstract: Creative intent in video editing can be expressed through text instructions (e.g., "remove the people"), image references (e.g., subject appearance), video references (e.g., camera movement), or a combination of the above. We introduce OmniXRef, a unified framework for multimodal multi-reference video editing that allows users to combine variable numbers of text, image, and video references to control diverse attributes of a source video. We first devise a unified input design with a reference-bank interface and introduce R^2-RoPE to support generalization to more references. Then our model, OmniXRef-Model, uses a single-stream diffusion transformer to jointly process the source video and multimodal context from an MLLM in an interleaved sequence. To address the scarcity of training data for video-reference editing, we construct OmniXRef-Data using synthesis pipelines for different editing tasks and combinations of references. We use curriculum learning to progressively increase task complexity and resolution. To support systematic evaluation of video as a control modality, we introduce OmniXRef-Bench, a benchmark for video-reference attribute transfer across Camera, Motion, Content, Style, and Visual Effects (VFX). Comprehensive evaluations show that our OmniXRef-Model outperforms task-specific baselines and commercial models.

title: Thermal activation of photon catalysis in difference-intensity Mach-Zehnder interferometry with squeezed thermal light
abstract: Realistic non-Gaussian operations, which can be implemented by mixing a nonclassical Gaussian state with a Fock state at a beam splitter and then heralding on a photon-number-resolving detector, are known to improve phase estimation in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. The existing studies have considered the single-mode squeezed vacuum for difference-intensity and parity detection, and the two-mode squeezed thermal state for parity detection alone as the initial Gaussian resources. However, a real squeezer in the lab actually produces single-mode squeezed thermal light, which has not been studied in a coherent-plus-resource interferometer. We take up this case and using the phase space Wigner picture, we obtain the heralded state produced by photon subtraction, addition and catalysis on a single-mode squeezed thermal resource, and evaluate the corresponding phase sensitivities. Single-photon catalysis, which is useless on squeezed vacuum, becomes a useful operation for any thermal occupation above $\nth\simeq0.2$, and since it heralds with a probability near one-half, it turns out to be the best success-weighted operation over the whole thermal range. In the vacuum limit our results reproduce the known hierarchy, where two-photon catalysis is the best operation. The quantum Fisher information computations confirms that thermal noise enhances the phase information encoded in the catalyzed state, demonstrating that difference-intensity detection closely approaches the ultimate precision bound across most operational regimes, and, together with a loss analysis, verifies the robustness of the effect.

title: The Delegation Dilemma: Economies of Scale, Accountability, and Polycentric Governance
abstract: Many collective-action systems are neither fully decentralized nor fully centralized: agents voluntarily organize into institutions that share organizational costs and delegate decisions to representatives. Delegation can reduce individual costs, but it also transfers control to representatives whose private objectives need not align with those of their constituents. We study this tension in a repeated game with endogenous delegation to self-interested centers. A simple reduced-form model yields a scale--accountability tradeoff: larger constituencies offer greater cost-sharing benefits to members, yet the marginal value to a center of retaining any one constituent decreases as group size grows. Consequently, the prospect of individual exit can sustain non-exploitative delegation only up to an endogenous accountable constituency size. Additionally, we identify parameter regions in which fully delegated, accountable governance, when feasible, must be polycentric. We investigate these predictions through simulations with large language model (LLM) agents. Across five matched pairs of 30-agent simulations, polycentric structures repeatedly emerge but remain fluid, exhibiting cycles of concentration, exploitation, exit, and re-formation. We further find that models of different capacity exhibit similar willingness to assume leadership but differ substantially in their exercise of authority, with Sol initiating exploitation more frequently than Luna in matched decision states.

title: A Comparison of Commonly Used Automatic Evaluation Metrics for Open-Ended Tasks in Portuguese
abstract: Open-ended tasks in Natural Language processing are characterized by the absence of a fixed set of outputs or short, predetermined responses. Typical examples include open-domain question answering and summarization. The automatic evaluation of these tasks is challenging, and existing metrics suffer from important limitations. Thus, many works have already been proposed to evaluate the performance of such metrics. However, the great majority of these works were conducted in English, leaving a gap for analyses in other languages, such as Portuguese. This work investigates the performance of some of the most popular automated intrinsic evaluation metrics for open-ended tasks by analyzing their correlation with human judgment. Using both the Summarization and Question Answering tasks, this study compares traditional n-gram-based metrics with metrics based on contextual embeddings generated by Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs), performing all analyses using models and datasets available for Portuguese. Results indicate that while PLM-based metrics generally show slightly higher correlation with human perception, their performance is highly reliant on the quality of the models used. Still, none of the evaluated metrics displayed a strong correlation with human judgments, suggesting the need for more robust metrics.

title: Student Questionnaire Dataset for Evaluating Chatbot Effectiveness in Academic Assistance
abstract: This dataset contains questionnaire responses collected to evaluate the effectiveness of chatbots in supporting students' academic activities. It is associated with the research paper entitled "Chatbot Effectiveness in Answering Student Inquiries for Academic Assistance." The questionnaire examines four constructs: Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU), Perceived Usefulness (PU), Intention to Use (ITU), and Actual Use (AU). The dataset also includes responses concerning chatbot usage patterns and academic use cases, alongside relevant respondent characteristics retained in anonymized form. The questionnaire uses a six-point Likert scale to measure respondents' perceptions and experiences. The dataset is intended to support research transparency, reproducibility, and further academic investigation into chatbot effectiveness and the use of conversational AI in educational settings. This dataset should be interpreted in conjunction with the associated research paper. Personally identifiable information should not be included in the publicly available version.

title: World Self-and-Mutual Modeling: An Adaptive Framework for Integrating Self-Modeling and Mutual Modeling into World Models
abstract: World models provide computational representations of environments and their dynamics, enabling systems to predict future states, evaluate hypothetical actions, and support planning. However, the development of a world model raises a broader architectural question: should a system primarily operate on its own internal representations, or should it interact with other models to improve its understanding of the world? Fixed reliance on either mode may be inefficient when environmental conditions, predictive uncertainty, task requirements, and computational resources change. This paper proposes the World Self-and-Mutual Model (WSMM), a conceptual framework that integrates self-modeling and mutual modeling into a world-model-based architecture. Self-modeling refers to the process through which a model independently examines, predicts with, evaluates, and updates its own representations. Mutual modeling refers to interactions among multiple models or model instances that exchange predictions, compare assumptions, identify discrepancies, and coordinate updates. WSMM introduces an adaptive meta-controller that selects self-modeling, mutual modeling, or hybrid operation according to estimated uncertainty, prediction errors, disagreement among models, expected information gain, and computational cost. The framework is intended to apply beyond large language models, including robotics, scientific simulation, autonomous systems, physical environments, digital twins, and general computational systems. This paper formalizes the proposed architecture, defines its operating modes, presents an adaptive switching algorithm, and develops a research methodology for empirical evaluation. It also distinguishes the proposal from established work on world models, self-modeling networks, multiple-model adaptive control, and multi-agent world modeling. The central research hypothesis is that adaptive coordination between self-modeling and mutual modeling may provide a better balance between predictive quality, computational efficiency, and robustness than fixed-mode alternatives. This hypothesis requires empirical validation.

title: Principles of Quantum Optimization for Constrained Problems
abstract: Constrained combinatorial optimization underlies many industrial and technological decision problems. In this talk, I will present a spectral theory that unifies many quantum optimization algorithms. I will show that computational slowdown is driven by entanglement restructuring: the creation, redistribution, and destruction of entanglement during system evolution. The severity of the slowdown depends on how much entanglement must be changed. I will show how algebraic properties of constraints induce such restructuring, and that constraint-aware dynamics reduce the associated slowdown by avoiding unnecessary restructuring. This framework explains why constraint-aware quantum methods can outperform generic penalty-based approaches. The theory connects constrained optimization, computational complexity, entanglement dynamics, and Hamiltonian spectral structure across continuous-time and circuit-based quantum optimization paradigms.

title: Lightweight anomaly detection via knowledge distillation from ensemble teachers
abstract: This paper proposes a knowledge distillation-based anomaly detection method that employs a heterogeneous Isolation Forest ensemble as the teacher and a lightweight neural network as the student. The student learns the teacher’s soft labels by minimizing the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence. Evaluated on three categories from the MVTec 3D-AD dataset (bagel, carrot, and cookie), the teacher achieves a macro-average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.6406, whereas the student, with 2.010 million parameters in the multilayer perceptron (MLP) head and an approximately 0.051 ms detector-head inference time per image (both excluding the ResNet-50 backbone), achieves a macro-average AUROC of 0.5937 and delivers an approximately 11.6-fold detector-head inference speedup over the teacher ensemble. Compared with representative deep learning baselines (RD4AD and PatchCore), the proposed method achieves moderate accuracy with lower detector-head latency and a smaller detector-head model footprint (excluding the backbone). These results suggest that knowledge distillation can serve as an effective compression technique, transferring ensemble knowledge to a lightweight student with a measurable accuracy trade-off. The benefit of distillation is category-dependent: the student outperforms the teacher on one category but exhibits performance degradation on the others. Moreover, the No-KD ablation (student trained without KD) achieves a higher macro-average AUROC (0.6057 vs. 0.5937), indicating that soft-label distillation is a viable compression strategy rather than a universal performance enhancer. The conditions under which distillation improves or degrades performance are discussed.

Compared with representative deep learning baselines (RD4AD and PatchCore), the proposed method achieves moderate accuracy with lower detector-head latency and a smaller detector-head model footprint (excluding the backbone). These results suggest that knowledge distillation can serve as an effective compression technique, transferring ensemble knowledge to a lightweight student with a measurable accuracy trade-off. The benefit of distillation is category-dependent: the student outperforms the teacher on one category but exhibits performance degradation on the others. Moreover, the No-KD ablation (student trained without KD) achieves a higher macro-average AUROC (0.6057 vs. 0.5937), indicating that soft-label distillation is a viable compression strategy rather than a universal performance enhancer. The conditions under which distillation improves or degrades performance are discussed.

title: TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents
abstract: Advances in frontier coding agents have sharply increased the token costs of AI-assisted software engineering. Their token efficiency is typically evaluated on isolated tasks, whereas real-world developers use them to continuously build, update, and maintain large-scale projects. This mismatch motivates us to evaluate agents over sequences of realistic coding tasks, where we find that agents exhibit recurring environment-dependent token costs that existing methods struggle to reduce. To minimize these costs, we introduce TokenEconomizer, an external controller that cuts environment-specific token costs over a sequence of tasks. These cuts come from determining (i) which operational micro-skills to inject, (ii) which persistently irrelevant tools to prune, and (iii) when to intervene in unproductive failure loops. Across Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot CLI paired with frontier models, TokenEconomizer reduces the average token cost by 18.4-30.9% with comparable task success. Savings hold in every repository under every tested agent-model setting and generalize to diverse domains such as sequential web development and security auditing, where costs fall by 6.4-21.2% depending on task structure. Our work establishes adaptive black-box cost control as a promising direction for reducing token costs of coding agents in realistic settings.

title: Not Just a Subject: Capturing Adaptive Scene-Specific Variance for Visual Storytelling
abstract: Recent advancements in diffusion models have significantly improved text-to-image generation, enabling their application to visual storytelling, where coherent image sequences are generated from narrative prompts. However, existing methods primarily focus on identity preservation and often fail to adapt to diverse scene variations, resulting in semantic misalignment and structural inflexibility. We propose EOS-Story, a training-free framework that harmonizes identity consistency with scene-specific adaptation across text and vision spaces. In the text space, we decouple the narrative into identity and scene sub-prompts to prevent information dilution, but this leaves the scene without access to appearance cues. To bridge this gap, we introduce Cross-Contextual Bridging, which softly injects a phrase-level appearance residual into the scene's <EOS> embedding. In the vision space, we find that scale mismatch between identity and scene subjects causes a few identity tokens to be repeatedly transferred, producing structural artifacts. We address this with Adaptive Identity Preservation, which anchors identity features at the scene-specific scale (Identity Anchoring) and integrates them via Identity-Aware Self-Attention. To evaluate performance under varied spatial compositions, we extend the Consistory+ benchmark with diverse framing scenarios (Consistory+_+). Extensive experiments show that EOS-Story achieves competitive or superior performance on both benchmarks.

title: Plans Are Not Executions: Adapting Frozen World-Model Planners to Controller-Induced Execution Shift
abstract: World-model planners evaluate candidate trajectories by predicting their future consequences, implicitly relying on the plan-to-motion relationship learned during training. At deployment, a different downstream controller may execute the same planned trajectory differently, creating a planning-execution gap between the frozen model's imagined future and actual execution. A natural remedy is to replace the planned trajectory with its predicted or observed execution. However, we find that better execution fidelity does not necessarily yield better decisions: directly substituting predicted execution trajectories yields only a 0.048 PDMS improvement across 10 unseen controller configurations, far smaller than the gain from our proposed adaptation. This suggests a semantic mismatch between a planned trajectory, which serves as a reference for downstream control, and an executed trajectory, which already describes the resulting post-controller motion. We introduce ExecutionBridge, which infers controller-specific execution characteristics from planned-executed trajectory pairs and uses them to adapt the native ego latent rollout while keeping the original planned trajectory unchanged. The planner, world model, and reward head remain frozen. On NAVSIM, ExecutionBridge consistently improves planning across unseen controller configurations and multiple frozen world-model planners, with substantially larger gains in challenging driving scenes where execution mismatch more strongly affects candidate evaluation.
